problem: The chapter states flatly that 'software risks fall into three families' and names product, process and technology. Standard textbooks use a different set of three (project, technical, business), and business risks — a budget cut, a customer withdrawing, a competitor shipping first — are never mentioned at all. A student who meets the standard taxonomy in the exam may think it contradicts this page.
fix: Say that most books group risks as project, technical and business, and that a common alternative grouping is product, process and technology; add one business-risk example (the customer cuts the budget mid-project) so no family is missing.

problem: 'One short meeting with the team and the tech lead usually finds the top ten risks in an afternoon' contradicts itself: a short meeting does not last an afternoon.
fix: One short meeting with the team and the tech lead usually fills the first draft of the risk list; the list is complete after an afternoon of checking it.

problem: The text allows impact in person-weeks or in rupees, but the formula and the table give I only in person-weeks and never say what the unit of RE is when I is in rupees. A student may write RE = 1.2 with no unit, or mix units inside one table.
fix: Add to the formula note: RE carries the unit of I, so if I is in rupees then RE is in rupees; every risk in one table must use the same unit.

problem: Calling an error budget 'a risk exposure for service downtime' is loose. An error budget is the amount of unreliability a service is allowed (1 minus the SLO), not a probability times an impact.
fix: An error budget is the amount of downtime a service is allowed to spend over a period, so it works like a pre-approved allowance for reliability risk.
